# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 59 — The EMET Bible (Literal)

**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** P.Mich. 130, Shepherd of Hermas 59 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_059_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 5, Part 5 — The Servant Who Does More Than Commanded

**59:1** I asked him further to explain to me all the parables and visions that I had seen. He said to me: "In all matters that I shall show you, I will explain them; only give me your whole heart and mind, and all the things I tell you will be explained."

**59:2** "The field," he said, "is this world; and the lord of the field is he who created all things and brought them to perfection and empowered them; and the son is the Holy Spirit; and the slave is the Son of God; and the vine is this people that he planted; and the fences are the holy angels of the Lord who protect his people; and the weeds that are pulled out of the vineyard are the transgressions of the servants of God; and the foods that he sent from the feast are the commandments that he gave to his people through his Son; and the friends and counselors are the holy angels who were first created; and the absence of the master is the time remaining before his coming."

**59:3** I said to him: "Lord, all things are great and marvelous and all things are glorious. Could I then have perceived these things?" He said to me: "No man who has God in his heart would have hesitated to ask, nor would he have failed to receive the explanation. But I will speak to you."

**59:4** "Now listen. The slave whom the master approved and made the principal heir of his possessions — that is the Son of God. The counselors are the first-created angels. But the absence of the master denotes the time remaining until his coming. The vine that is cultivated is the people of God. The fences are the angels who guard the people. The weeds pulled out are the sins of the servants. The foods sent from the feast are the commandments given through the Son. The friends are the prophets who served God."

---

*EMET renders the Greek of P.Mich. 130 with maximal literalness, preserving the full allegorical key to the vineyard parable.*
